content: The term atomic battery refers to a device that generates electricity by utilizing the emissions from a radioactive isotope. These devices, also known as nuclear batteries, tritium batteries, or radioisotope batteries, convert the energy released during natural radioactive decay directly into electrical energy. The concept of nuclear battery technology dates back to 1913, when Henry Moseley first demonstrated the Beta Cell. Significant research into these batteries occurred during the 1950s and 1960s, particularly for applications requiring long-lasting power sources in space exploration. Over time, various designs and methods have been developed, with advancements in nanotechnology and wide-bandgap semiconductors enabling the creation of new devices with enhanced material properties. Modern atomic batteries are being developed internationally to provide long-lived power sources, typically lasting 10 to 20 years, by harnessing the energy from radioisotope decay. Conversion techniques for these batteries are categorized into two main types: thermal and non-thermal. Thermal converters, such as thermoelectric and thermionic generators, rely on temperature differentials to produce power. Non-thermal converters, on the other hand, extract energy directly from radioactive decay without relying on temperature differences. Thermal Converters 1. Thermionic Converters: A thermionic converter consists of a hot electrode that emits electrons thermionically across a space charge barrier to a cooler electrode, generating useful power. Cesium vapor is often used to optimize the work functions of the electrodes and provide an ion supply to neutralize the electron space charge. 2. Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTGs): Thermoelectric converters use pairs of thermocouples connected in series. Each thermocouple is formed by the junction of two dissimilar materials, with one side heated and the other cooled. While metal thermocouples have low thermal-to-electrical efficiency, semiconductor materials like bismuth telluride and silicon-germanium can achieve much higher conversion efficiencies due to their adjustable carrier density and charge properties. 3. Thermophotovoltaic Cells: These cells operate similarly to photovoltaic cells but convert infrared light emitted by a hot surface into electricity. Thermophotovoltaic cells have slightly higher efficiency than thermoelectric couples and can be combined with them to potentially double the overall efficiency. Research at the University of Houston aims to integrate thermophotovoltaic cells with thermocouples, achieving a 3to 4-fold improvement in system efficiency compared to current RTGs. 4. Alkali-Metal Thermal-to-Electric Converters (AMTEC): AMTEC systems are electrochemical devices based on sodium-beta-alumina solid electrolytes. These systems use a sodium concentration cell, with sodium vapor at high pressure (900–1300 K) on one side and liquid sodium at low pressure (400–700 K) on the other. Laboratory efficiencies for AMTEC cells have reached 16%, with predictions of up to 20%. Non-Thermal Converters Non-thermal converters extract a fraction of nuclear energy as it degrades into heat, without relying on temperature differences. These systems are divided into three main classes: 1. Direct Charging Generators: These generators use a capacitor charged by the current of charged particles (e.g., beta or alpha particles) emitted from a radioactive layer. While this method dates back to 1913, its practical applications have been limited due to the low currents and high voltages produced. Oscillator/transformer systems are often employed to reduce the voltage, followed by rectifiers to convert the power back to direct current. 2. Betavoltaics: Betavoltaic devices generate electricity by capturing beta particles emitted during radioactive decay. In 2005, researchers from the University of Rochester and the University of Toronto developed a small battery powered by tritium decay, suitable for pacemakers and low-current household devices. This technology, which operates similarly to photovoltaic cells, has the potential to significantly improve the efficiency and energy density of atomic batteries. 3. Optoelectric Nuclear Batteries: Proposed by researchers at the Kurchatov Institute in Moscow, this design uses a beta-emitter (e.g., technetium-99) to stimulate an excimer mixture, producing light that powers a photocell. The battery consists of an excimer mixture (argon/xenon) in a pressure vessel with an internal mirrored surface, finely divided technetium-99, and an ultrasonic stirrer. This design eliminates the need for precision electrode assemblies and allows most beta particles to contribute to the battery's net power. 4. Reciprocating Electromechanical Atomic Batteries: These batteries utilize the electrostatic charge buildup between two plates to create mechanical motion. A flexible plate is pulled toward a fixed plate until contact is made, discharging the accumulated charge and springing back. The mechanical motion can generate electricity through piezoelectric materials or linear generators. These systems produce milliwatts of power in pulses, depending on the charge rate, with frequencies reaching up to 35 Hz. Radioisotopes Used Atomic batteries typically use radioisotopes that emit low-energy beta particles or, in some cases, alpha particles. Low-energy beta particles are preferred to minimize the production of high-energy Bremsstrahlung radiation, which would require heavy shielding. Commonly tested radioisotopes include tritium, nickel-63, promethium-147, and technetium-99. Other isotopes, such as plutonium-238, curium-242, curium-244, and strontium-90, have also been used in various applications. In Fiction Atomic batteries have appeared in various fictional works. In the live-action Batman TV series, the Batmobile is powered by atomic batteries, as referenced in Robin's checklist: Atomic batteries to power. Turbines to speed. Similarly, in the animated Justice League series, a nuclear battery from a JLA communicator plays a role in a time-travel rescue mission. In the video game Wing Commander 3, spacecraft are powered by atomic batteries, using the same phrase from the Batman series. In the French cartoon Code Lyoko, the supercomputer is powered by a nuclear battery, speculated by fans to be uranium-based, though this is unlikely given the battery's apparent 20-year lifespan.
